units.title: What Are We Living For?
units.sub: A survivor of Auschwitz, philosophers who did not believe in God, and the book of Ecclesiastes are all asking the same question.

share.v: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts

blocks.h: In 1945, in a subcamp of a concentration camp in southern Germany, a Viennese doctor sat with small scraps of paper he had gotten from the camp office, rewriting from memory the manuscript that had been taken from him.

His father, his mother, his brother and his wife did not walk out of that catastrophe alive. The following year he spent only nine days dictating a book, which in the English-speaking world became known as Man’s Search for Meaning. A man who had lost almost everything wrote about this: why a person can still go on living.
That question is far older than Auschwitz. There is a book in the Bible that asks it for us right from its opening:
“Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
Three serious answers

The first: living on itself needs a “why.” The Jewish psychiatrist Viktor Frankl observed in the camp that those who held on often still had something unfinished, or someone waiting for them. He quoted Nietzsche: a person who knows why he lives can bear almost any how. He later summed up three ways of finding meaning: creating a work or giving yourself to one, loving a person, and the attitude we choose when we face suffering we cannot change.

The second: the universe gives no answer. In 1882 Nietzsche’s madman asked in the marketplace: who gave us the sponge to wipe away the whole horizon? Are we not straying through an infinite nothing? His point was that the consequences of the West losing God would be far more serious than people of his day imagined. Albert Camus, at the opening of The Myth of Sisyphus in 1942, put it even more directly, calling whether life is worth living the one truly serious philosophical problem. His own answer: do not give up; live with clear eyes, and revolt against the absurd.

If you are thinking right now that you do not want to live: thank you for still reading. This thought is very heavy, and you do not have to carry it alone. Tell someone you trust today, and please seek professional help as well. In Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925 (24 hours, free of charge) or Lifeline 1995; if the call does not connect, try again or switch to the other number. Elsewhere, please find your local crisis line; if there is immediate danger, call your local emergency number or go to an emergency room.

The third: meaning can be established within the human world. Many serious non-believers today do not feel that their lives are empty. They live for family, for justice, for art, for serving others, and they live movingly. This testimony deserves respect.

A key can serve as a bookmark, a letter opener, or a charm hanging on a backpack. None of these uses is wrong, and you may even enjoy them. But if it was originally the key to a particular door, then one day you will want to know: where is that door? Here is the question: is my whole life a piece of metal for me to use as I please, or is there a door it was made to open?
Can money buy satisfaction but not meaning?

An analysis of Gallup data covering 132 countries and more than 140,000 people found that people in wealthier countries are more satisfied with life but rate their lives as less meaningful, while in poorer countries it is the opposite. The researchers suggested that the strength of religious belief may be one of the key factors. This is a correlation. Poverty itself is nothing to envy, but the finding reminds us that “doing well” and “living meaningfully” are two different things.

An American study that followed nearly 7,000 adults over age 50 found that, over four years, the group with the lowest sense of purpose in life had about 2.4 times the risk of death of the group with the highest. This is a correlation and cannot establish cause, and it certainly does not mean that people who become ill or die early lacked purpose.

In 1971 Thomas Nagel offered a subtle analysis: the sense of absurdity comes from a conflict within a person. We take our lives seriously, and yet we can always step back and doubt how much it all weighs. He thought this is not worth despair, nor does it call for heroic posturing; one can face it with a touch of irony. Susan Wolf argued that meaning arises when subjective engagement meets objectively worthwhile things, and her discussion deliberately does not presuppose God.
Let us separate the statements and mark how certain each one is.

Frankl was sent to a concentration camp in 1942 and was freed in 1945; his parents, brother and wife all died in the catastrophe. In 1946 he dictated, in nine days, his book about his camp experience.

A 2021 Pew Research Center survey of 17 advanced economies: in 14 of them the most commonly mentioned source of meaning was family; in Taiwan the most commonly mentioned was society (convenient living, national health insurance, freedom and so on); apart from the United States, the share mentioning religion was no higher than 5% anywhere.

Cross-national data show that wealth is positively correlated with life satisfaction but negatively correlated with self-rated meaning in life; religiosity may be a mediating factor. This is survey data from 2007, and the question of causation remains open for discussion.
A higher sense of purpose in life is associated with lower mortality; whether it is causal is not settled.

People widely long for a meaning beyond themselves. This may point to a Creator who gives meaning, or it may be, as Camus and Nagel put it, only a gap between humans and the world. The longing itself cannot prove God; it can only make us take that possibility seriously.
The viewpoint conversation room
Philosophers divide this question roughly into several positions. Below they are set side by side, each in its strongest form.

items.h: If there is a God who creates and loves people, life’s meaning has a foundation that does not fade with time. The biggest challenge: is this just pushing the question up one level? Even God’s purpose, why does it count as meaningful?

Love, knowledge, beauty and the reduction of suffering have real value within a finite life and need no eternity to endorse them. A concert does not lose its value because it ends. The biggest challenge: where does the objectivity of these values come from, and how do we face the final cold silence of the universe?
The conditions for life’s meaning simply cannot be met. Few people manage to live this view all the way through, but it honestly asks the question that both of the other views must answer.

blocks.h: Where is the door?

The most honest thing about Ecclesiastes is that it lets a person finish speaking his despair; even words like “so I hated life” were kept in the canon. God does not ask you to pretend you are not tired. But the author sees one more thing at the same time: inside a person there is a space larger than “under the sun.”
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
The New Testament tells us the name of that door. Your existence has an object, and that object is a Lord with a name.

For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him.
Asked about the greatest commandment, Jesus gathered life into two directions: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself. Here meaning takes the shape of relationship.

Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’

The first question of the Westminster Shorter Catechism, which the Christian church has passed down for centuries, answers the same way: the chief end of man is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever.

And this Lord personally walked into the emptiness. He died for our sins and rose from the dead. “Under the sun” is no longer the last word, so all the love and labor that looked wasted have somewhere to go.
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.
Take a sheet of paper and write down the three things that took the most of your time last week. Beside each one ask: for whom was this done? No need to rush to change anything. Just look honestly.
Meditate: if tomorrow no one praises me anymore, will I still know why I live? Can my “why” hold the weakness and aging of a person?

Prayer: Lord Jesus, who created me and gave Your life for me, I confess that I often cover the emptiness in my heart with busyness. Thank You for not rebuking me because I asked, “What am I living for?” Be my reason for living Yourself, lead me to love You with all my heart and to love the people around me. If anyone is so tired right now that he does not want to walk any further, draw near to him and send someone to accompany him. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Let Jesus reign: hand the steering wheel of your life to the Lord who made me and died for me. My plans may be adjusted, but His love does not change.
Shift your viewpoint: move from a human, temporary view to God’s eternal view. A small visit that looks insignificant today is not in vain in the Lord.
People matter more than tasks: those who love God with all their heart will put that love into the person right in front of them, and this is what meaning looks like most concretely.

blocks.h: This week: write a one-sentence “living declaration” beginning with “I live for…” and put it in your phone’s notes. A week later, look back at how much of it actually shows up in your calendar.
Pass it on: if you set aside what others expect of you, what would make you say in old age, “This life was worth it”?
Quiz

quiz.q: Which of the following does Frankl count among the ways of finding meaning?
o: Accumulating enough wealth
The attitude we choose when facing suffering we cannot change
Not thinking about life’s questions at all
quiz.e: He mentioned work, love, and the attitude toward suffering.

quiz.q: What did Oishi and Diener’s analysis of data from 132 countries find?
o: People in wealthier countries are more satisfied with life but rate their lives as less meaningful
Poverty is the secret of happiness
Rich people must be emptier
quiz.e: This is a country-level correlation. It reminds us that satisfaction and meaning are two different things; it cannot be inferred to individuals, and it is no praise of poverty.

quiz.q: According to Colossians 1:16, what is the relationship between all things and Christ?
o: All things have nothing to do with Him
He created only the visible world
All things were created through Him and for Him
quiz.e: The object of life’s meaning is a Lord with a name.

units.title: Suffering: Where Is God?
units.sub: The best thing Job’s friends ever did was sit in silence for seven days. This lesson first sits down beside you, and only then slowly begins to talk.

share.v: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

blocks.h: The best thing Job’s three friends ever did was to say nothing for seven whole days.
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.
On the eighth day they began to explain. They explained for more than thirty chapters, each one quoting his authorities. At the end of the book, this is what God said about them:

It was so, that after Yahweh had spoken these words to Job, Yahweh said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.

If you are in the middle of suffering, this lesson will not ask you to figure it all out quickly. You can just sit for now. If you want to cry, or get angry, or close this page halfway through, that is all right.
The most important thing first

If you are thinking right now that you do not want to live: thank you for still reading. This thought is very heavy. It does not mean you are weak, and it does not mean you have no faith. Tell someone you trust today, and seek professional help. In Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925 or Lifeline 1995; if the call does not connect, try again or switch to the other number. Elsewhere, please find your local crisis line; if there is immediate danger, call your local emergency number.

If your suffering was inflicted on you by someone else (domestic violence, sexual assault, long-term humiliation), it is not your fault, and no one should tell you to put up with it a little longer. Go first to a safe place and tell someone you trust. In Taiwan you can call the 113 Protection Hotline.
Three things that sound spiritual but really hurt

“There must be a reason. You should reflect.” This is exactly the logic of Job’s friends: a person who suffers must have done something wrong. Jesus’ disciples once thought the same way, and when they saw a man born blind they asked who had sinned. Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents.” When He spoke about the tower that fell and killed eighteen people, He also denied that they were worse offenders than anyone else (Luke 13:4-5).

“It’s all part of God’s good plan.” The Bible says that all things work together for good for those who love God. What Paul speaks of is God’s final work; he did not say that every single event is good in itself, and he himself wrote of death as an enemy. To bring this sentence into a funeral hall is to speak for God words He has not spoken to this person.
We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.

A traditional Chinese herbal prescription may contain huanglian (goldthread), and however good the prescription, huanglian taken alone is still bitter. No one calls it sweet just because the prescription is good. Even less would anyone walk up to a patient who is vomiting and lecture him on pharmacology. Romans 8:28 is a prescription, and God is the one who writes it. What the companion should be holding is a cup of warm water.

“Time heals everything.” The philosopher Nicholas Wolterstorff’s 25-year-old son Eric died in a mountain-climbing accident. In Lament for a Son (1987) he frankly said that he did not know why God watched his son fall. Twelve years later he said that the wound was no longer so raw, but it was still there.
The language the Bible gives us: lament

Psalm 88 almost never clears from beginning to end. Most other laments turn toward praise at the close, but the last word of this one (in Hebrew) is “darkness.” A nineteenth-century commentator called it unique among the psalms, with the darkness running all the way to the end. God put this psalm in the Bible.
LORD, why do you reject my soul? Why do you hide your face from me?

C. S. Lewis’s wife Joy died of cancer in 1960. In 1961 he published A Grief Observed under a pseudonym, honestly recording his anger and bewilderment toward God: crying out felt like running into a door bolted from the inside. Later in the book his feelings change, but he never said he had figured it out.

Joni Eareckson Tada was injured in a diving accident on July 30, 1967, and has been a quadriplegic since the age of 17; she later went through stage-three breast cancer and severe chronic pain. She reminds the church that the original meaning of the word compassion is “to suffer together.” In reviewing Timothy Keller’s book on suffering she also noted that, for someone who clenches a fist and asks “why,” the answer itself can hurt.
Being angry with God is common

A 2011 study by the psychologist Julie Exline and colleagues found that anger toward God after negative events is not uncommon (positive feelings toward God are still more common). This anger was linked to poorer adjustment to bereavement and cancer, and the link was strongest when the anger had gone unresolved for a year. This is a correlation and does not mean your anger harmed you. The more sensible reading is this: do not keep it bottled up; bring it to God, and bring it to people who can talk with you.
A harder question: does God suffer?

In Night, Elie Wiesel recorded the scene in the camp of a child being hanged: someone asked where God was, and a voice within him answered that He was right here, hanging on this gallows. Interpreters read this line very differently: some read it as an image of sacrifice, others as the death of God. Wiesel was Jewish, and he cannot be read as a Christian witness.

The German theologian Jürgen Moltmann was drafted at 16 and was a prisoner of war from 1945 to 1948; in the camp he received a New Testament for the first time. In The Crucified God (English translation 1974) he argued that on the cross God personally bore human suffering. This claim challenged the church tradition’s doctrine that God’s nature cannot suffer, and it set off a long debate.
In suffering, facts cannot replace comfort, but they should not be replaced by comfort either. We separate what is certain from what is inferred.
Psalm 88 as a whole is mostly a plea, the ending does not turn to praise, and it is often regarded as the darkest of the psalms.

Lewis’s A Grief Observed was published in 1961 under the pseudonym N. W. Clerk, written after his wife Joy died of cancer; Wolterstorff’s Lament for a Son was published in 1987, written after his 25-year-old son died in a mountaineering accident.

Anger toward God is common after negative events and is associated with poorer adjustment to bereavement and cancer, most strongly when it stays unresolved over a long time. This is correlational research, and the direction of cause must be treated with caution.

“God is with us in suffering” is a declaration of faith, and science cannot measure it. Many honest people stop believing in God precisely because of suffering, and that struggle deserves respect; for the philosophical discussion of this question, see the next unit.
Christians believe that God will in the end wipe away every tear. This is a hope grounded in Christ’s resurrection, and it does not make today’s pain any less real.
The viewpoint conversation room
How is God “with us” in suffering? Within evangelicalism and the historic church there are different ways of putting it, each with its strongest reasons.

items.n: God’s nature cannot suffer (the classical tradition)
items.h: God is not swayed by His creatures, so His love cannot be shaken by suffering, and that is why He is able to save. The one who suffered was the incarnate Son, who truly suffered in His humanity. Thomas Weinandy is a representative author. The challenge: does this sound too distant?

Moltmann argued that a God who cannot suffer also cannot love. The cross is an event that the Father and the Son bear together in love. The challenge: can a God who is trapped by suffering as we are still save us?

Both sides affirm that Jesus is truly God and truly man, that His suffering was real, and that He is not far from those who suffer. The main disagreement is how to describe God’s nature, and this should never be a reason to hold anyone back from pouring out their grief to God.

blocks.h: Jesus did not explain first

Lazarus had been dead four days, and Mary came weeping to Jesus. Jesus knew that in a few minutes He would call Lazarus out, and on that road He was the one most qualified to give an explanation. What the Bible records is this:

When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept.
Even the One who knew the ending wept. So your weeping now does not mean your faith is not enough.
He walked in
God has not told us all the reasons for suffering. The response He gave is a person: Christ, God made flesh. Isaiah described Him this way hundreds of years earlier:

He was despisedand rejected by men, a man of sufferingand acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sicknessand carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.

In Taiwanese hospitals there is a kind of bedside chair for the companion, narrow and hard, which can just about be unfolded into a bed. The person who stays in it usually cannot solve anything; he cannot read the reports, and he cannot feel the pain for you. But when you wake in the middle of the night and turn your head and see someone curled up there, in that moment you know you have not been abandoned. Christ did more: He did not stay in the companion’s chair. He lay down on the hospital bed.
He died on the cross for our sins and rose on the third day. His risen body still bore the nail marks, and He invited doubting Thomas to touch them with his own hand.
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Your Lord has wounds too. When you bring Him your complaints, the One across from you is not a counselor who has never been hurt.
At the end of justice and tears

Here God’s goodness is joined to His justice: He does not count the victim’s wounds against the victim, and He will not tolerate evil forever. Hope cannot make today stop hurting. It only says: the pain is not the last word.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.”

For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Take a sheet of paper and write four lines of your own lament. Line one: “God, I…” Line two: “Why did You…” Line three: “I need…” Line four: “I still say to You…” If you cannot write the fourth line, leave it blank; Psalm 88 did not write it either.
Meditate: what is the one question I most want to ask God right now? Have I been afraid to ask it out loud because I thought it would be irreverent?

Prayer: Lord Jesus, You wept at Lazarus’s tomb, and Your body bears wounds. I do not really know how to pray, so I hand You these tears and questions. I do not want anyone to explain You to me; I want You to come near. Send me someone who can accompany me, and give me the courage to ask for help. If someone is so tired tonight that he does not want to walk any further, keep watch over him, and let him tell someone today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Jesus is my example: He wept first and spoke afterward. The next time you meet someone who is suffering, put your answers away and learn to ask as He did: “Will you take me to see?”
People matter more than tasks: being with someone is often inefficient and solves no problems. Treat the person as someone to accompany, not a case to fix.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry: if you are suffering, setting your service aside for a while or not leading a small group is not a step backward. God wants you, the person.

blocks.h: This week: think of someone who is grieving, long-term ill or out of work, and send them one line: “I don’t know what to say, but I remember you. Can I come and sit with you for a while this week?” No Bible verse, no advice. If the one who is suffering is you, read your four-line lament to someone you trust.
Pass it on: “In the hardest stretch of your life, what is the one thing someone did that helped the most? Which sentence was the hardest to bear?”
Quiz

quiz.q: In which period are Job’s friends’ actions most worth learning from?
o: When they began quoting authorities on the eighth day
When they sat with him seven days and nights without speaking
When they rebuked Job for hiding sin
quiz.e: Their silent presence in chapter 2 was far better than their later explanations; in 42:7 God also rebuked their arguments.

quiz.q: How did Jesus answer the question “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
o: This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents
It was his parents’ sin
It was his sin in a previous life
quiz.e: John 9:3. Suffering must never be blamed across the board on the one who suffers.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the most fitting statement about Romans 8:28?
o: Every bad thing is good in itself
Those who suffer should immediately give thanks for disaster
It proclaims God’s final work and should not be used to interrupt another’s grief
quiz.e: This is a true promise, but the timing and manner of using it matter greatly. Romans 12:15 also teaches us to weep with those who weep.

units.title: If God Is Good, Why Is There Evil?
units.sub: One of the strongest objections to Christianity came from the pen of a Christian novelist. We will read it through to the end.

share.v: Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

blocks.h: One of the strongest arguments against Christianity was written by a Christian novelist.

In The Brothers Karamazov, Fyodor Dostoevsky has Ivan list, one after another, children who were tortured though innocent, and then tells his devout younger brother Alyosha: even if there is to be an eternal harmony one day, if the price of admission is the unavenged tears of a single child, he will return his ticket. Ivan says he does not deny that God exists. What he refuses to accept is the ticket.
Dostoevsky did not write this passage weakly. Neither does the Bible. The prophet Habakkuk had asked the same thing long before:

LORD, how long will I cry, and you will not hear? I cry out to you “Violence!” and will you not save? Why do you show me iniquity, and look at perversity? For destruction and violence are before me. There is strife, and contention rises up.
This question has two versions

A passage we often hear goes like this: if God wants to remove evil but cannot, He is not all-powerful; if He can but will not, He is not all-good; if He both can and will, where does evil come from? This is often said to come from Epicurus, but it cannot be found in his surviving writings. The earliest to attribute it to him was the Christian author Lactantius, and David Hume’s Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) made it widely known.

The logical version. In 1955 the Australian philosopher J. L. Mackie argued that the coexistence of an all-powerful, all-good God and evil is logically contradictory, so theism is irrational. In God, Freedom, and Evil (1974), Alvin Plantinga offered the free will defense: creatures with real freedom, able to do good and also evil, may be a greater good; even an all-powerful God cannot make people freely do only good, since that is a contradiction. He needed only to show that the two claims are not contradictory, and did not have to say what God’s actual reasons are. Today the academic community broadly holds that this defense successfully answered the logical version of that time. Mackie himself admitted in 1982 that it was no longer a contradiction, though he doubted whether that counts as a real solution.

The evidential version. This is the real battlefield today. In 1979 William Rowe described a scene: lightning sets a forest on fire, a fawn is terribly burned and lies in agony alone for days before it dies, and no one ever knows. He asked: what greater good could such suffering bring? Since we cannot see any, there probably is none, and so there probably is no all-good God. Later discussion added a real case: the murder of a five-year-old child. His argument does not say God cannot exist, only that it is “unlikely.” This argument remains one of the heaviest challenges to theism, and neither side has settled it completely.

The logical version is like an auditor saying: this ledger cannot possibly balance, so there must be fraud. As soon as someone produces one possible way of calculating that makes it balance, the accusation is withdrawn. The evidential version is like an auditor saying: perhaps there is a way to calculate it, but I have gone through so many entries and cannot make sense of a single one; is this company really honest? That is harder to answer, because he is pointing at every real entry before our eyes.
Several Christian responses

Not seeing is not the same as not being there. In 1984 Stephen Wykstra pointed out that if such a God exists, it is no surprise that His reasons lie beyond our sight, just as a baby cannot understand why his mother carries him to get a shot. Rowe’s reply was also powerful: a loving mother stays beside her child during the shot and lets the child feel her love, and does not disappear. Many who suffer do not feel God. This response and rebuttal bring us to the “Reveal” step below.

Soul-making. In 1966 John Hick argued that the world is a place for shaping souls, and that an easy life cannot produce courage and compassion. Critics ask: what about those who are utterly crushed by suffering? What about children who die young?

General reasons are not enough. The Oxford theologian Marilyn McCord Adams pointed out in Horrendous Evils and the Goodness of God (1999) that, for someone who has met devastating evil, “the whole world is better for it” is no answer. The problem has to be resolved within that person’s own life, and she pointed especially to God’s becoming human Himself and bearing it together with people.
The line of evil runs through whose heart

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, a survivor of the Soviet labor camps, wrote in The Gulag Archipelago that the line dividing good and evil does not pass between states, classes or parties, but through every human heart. He worked this out in prison. The Bible’s diagnosis of evil is equally unsparing:

For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts, covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness. All these evil things come from within and defile the man.”
This passage speaks of the tendencies inside each one of us. It must never be used to tell a victim, “you share in it too.” Perpetrator and victim must be kept apart.
Without God, is “evil” still evil?

Some Christian philosophers ask in return: if there is no God, what is the ground for saying “this is objectively evil”? Mackie himself held that objective moral facts do not exist (1977). But let us be fair: there are also serious atheist philosophers who hold that moral truths are themselves basic facts and need no God, for example Erik Wielenberg. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on moral arguments also says that such arguments are not “proofs,” and that every premise can reasonably be denied. So this shows only that both sides have homework to do, and it cannot be used to claim victory.
This question easily turns into a quarrel, so let us mark clearly how certain each statement is.
Mackie raised the logical problem of evil in 1955; Plantinga offered the free will defense in 1974; Rowe raised the evidential version in 1979.

The academic community broadly holds that Plantinga answered the logical version of the mid-twentieth century. But this means only “not contradictory.” It does not answer why evil is so great in amount and so heavy in weight, and free will does not necessarily suffice to account for earthquakes and disease.

Whether the evidential version succeeds is still debated: skeptical theists question the inference “if we cannot see a reason, there may be no reason”; their opponents think this would undermine other knowledge and moral judgments as well.
Whether evil presupposes an objective good that exists only if God does is a contested philosophical inference, not a proof; both theistic and atheistic moral realism have serious defenders.

Christians believe that on the cross God personally bore evil and that He will one day judge justly. This does not explain where evil comes from, and it cannot be verified by argument. It is a declaration of faith based on Jesus’ resurrection.
The viewpoint conversation room
Below are the strongest versions set side by side, all from serious scholars.

items.h: Real love and goodness require real freedom, and freedom opens the possibility of evil. Its strength is explaining human-caused evil; its weakness is earthquakes, disease, and why God does not intervene a bit more.
The world is a school for growth. Its strength is that it fits the testimony of many who have come through suffering; its weakness is those who were destroyed and never had time to grow.

Finite human beings should not assume they can understand all of God’s reasons. Its strength is pointing out a gap in the inference; its weakness is that it may leave people unable to trust moral judgments as well, and it is hard to comfort those who suffer.

The world has so much seemingly pointless suffering that “the universe does not care” explains it more simply than “there is an all-good God” (compare Paul Draper, 1989). The challenge: how to explain why people cannot accept this “not caring,” and what grounds moral anger.

Christianity offers no complete list of reasons. It proclaims that God personally entered the deepest place of evil. This cannot replace the discussion above, and it will not make the questioning disappear.

blocks.h: God’s answer is a person

After hearing Ivan’s accusation, Alyosha did not argue that those children do not deserve sympathy. He raised only one thing: there is an innocent victim in the world who shed blood, and He has the right to speak. Here Dostoevsky places the Christian response.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

Here God’s goodness takes on weight. Christ was betrayed, wrongly condemned and tortured; all this happened to Him. He bore our sins, and He rose from the dead. This does not explain where evil comes from, but it tells us which side God is on.
He will judge
A universe without judgment is good news only for the perpetrator. The victims in the Bible do not ask God to “let it go”; they ask, “How long?”

When he opened the fifth seal, I saw underneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed for the Word of God, and for the testimony of the Lamb which they had. They cried with a loud voice, saying, “How long, Master, the holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”

The Croatian theologian Miroslav Volf wrote Exclusion and Embrace (1996) out of his reflection on the war in Yugoslavia. He argued that people can refuse to answer violence with violence only by believing that the final judgment is in God’s hands. Abraham asked as well, “Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?” That question is still valid today.
Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.” Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

Please read this passage carefully. “Don’t seek revenge yourselves” (12:19) does not mean not calling the police, not seeking help, or staying in the violence. The first thing for someone being harmed is safety; in Taiwan you can call the 113 Protection Hotline. Overcoming evil with good does not include keeping the perpetrator’s secrets.

As for why God has not yet ended all this, Scripture gives only a little light: He is still waiting for people to repent. For the victim this is not necessarily an immediate comfort, and we need not pretend it is.
The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

Open today’s news and pick one thing that makes you angry. Stay inside that anger for one minute, without rushing to explain it. Then ask yourself: this feeling of “this is not right,” do I think it is real?
Meditate: the thing I have recently blamed others for, has that line also run through my own heart? Have I ever used the language of faith to tell a victim to be quiet?

Prayer: Righteous Lord, the evil in the world makes us angry and makes us confused. What we do not understand, please do not let us pretend to understand. Thank You that You did not stand far away; on the cross You bore it Yourself. Comfort the victims, restrain those who do evil, and search my own heart. Lord, come quickly and do justice. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Humility overcomes pride: in the face of this question you may say “I don’t know.” Before a doubting friend, honesty is more like Christ than winning the debate.

Self-centered and selfless: I have a share in the root of evil. Before asking about others, ask yourself: what bit of power am I gripping and refusing to let go that is hurting someone? (This is for self-examination, not an assignment for victims.)
The Bible is my standard: let Habakkuk and Revelation teach me how to cry out to God about injustice, and let Romans 12 teach me not to repay evil with evil.

blocks.h: This week: do one concrete small act of overcoming evil with good: support an organization that protects victims, accompany a friend who is going through legal proceedings, or admit your wrong to someone you have hurt.
Pass it on: “What do you think is the one thing in this world that makes people doubt God the most? If you are willing, I would like to hear you out; I don’t think there is a simple answer either.”
Quiz

quiz.q: About the “Epicurean paradox,” which statement is correct?
o: The passage cannot be found in his surviving works; attributing it to him is a later claim
It is a line from his own book
Christians made it up in order to refute themselves
quiz.e: The earliest to attribute it to Epicurus was Lactantius, and Hume made it popular in 1779.

quiz.q: What question does Plantinga’s free will defense mainly answer?
o: Why there is so much evil
The specific reason for each suffering
Whether an all-powerful, all-good God and evil are logically contradictory
quiz.e: He needed only to show that they are not contradictory, which is not the same as solving all suffering.

quiz.q: How should “Don’t seek revenge yourselves” in Romans 12 be understood when applied to those suffering violence?
o: You must not call the police
Do not take revenge by lynching, but you may and should seek safety, help and legal protection
Stay where you are and keep enduring
quiz.e: The text forbids repaying evil with evil, not asking for help. The first priority for someone being abused is safety.

units.title: Death: The Last Enemy
units.sub: We can take the fourth floor off the elevator buttons, but we cannot take that floor out of life.

share.v: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.

blocks.h: We can take the fourth floor off the elevator buttons, but we cannot take that floor out of life.

On March 6, 1974, the cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker died of colon cancer at the age of 49. Two months later his book won the Pulitzer Prize. Its title was The Denial of Death. He argued that a very large part of human civilization has been built so that we do not have to look at this one thing.
The Bible long ago asked people to look.
It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting; for that is the end of all men, and the living should take this to heart.
The most important thing first

If you are thinking right now that you do not want to live: please read this paragraph first. The hope of resurrection is never a reason to leave early; your life today is precious in God’s eyes. Tell someone you trust today, and seek professional help. In Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925 or Lifeline 1995; if the call does not connect, try again or switch to the other number. Elsewhere, please find your local crisis line; if there is immediate danger, call your local emergency number.

If you have just lost someone you love, you can read this lesson slowly. You do not need to look strong, and you do not need to have words of faith ready right away. If your loved one died by suicide, this is not something you should carry alone. Please do not accept words like “he must be in hell.” A person’s eternity is in God’s hands; He is more merciful and more just than we are, and He knows all the pain of that person’s last moments. Please also find someone who knows how to walk with the bereaved.
How we dodge it

Becker held that careers, reputations, the next generation, and great causes can all become a person’s “immortality projects,” making him feel that he will outlast his body. The Chinese versions are many too: avoiding the number four, saying “passed away” instead of “died,” putting off a will until it cannot be put off any longer. When Confucius was asked about death, he said only: not yet understanding life, how can you understand death? (Analects, Book 11). The ancient philosopher Epicurus said that death is nothing to us, because when we are here it is not, and when it is here we are not. This is a very strong comfort for those who do not believe in an afterlife, and it deserves respect.

In the mango orchards of central and southern Taiwan, while the whole tree is still green, one mango always turns yellow first. The grower sees that one and knows: this tree is about to ripen. Paul says that Christ rose from the dead as the “first fruit,” meaning that His is not an exception. It is the beginning of the whole tree.
Grief is not climbing stairs

Many people have heard of the “five stages”: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. They come from Elisabeth Kübler-Ross’s On Death and Dying (1969), which was about terminally ill patients, not the bereaved, and she herself said that patients often go through two or three stages at once and not necessarily in order. In 2017 Margaret Stroebe and colleagues reviewed the evidence and argued that stage theory lacks solid empirical support and may even harm people who do not follow that order.
Closer to the research is the “dual process model”: the bereaved swing back and forth between facing the loss and rebuilding life, and both are necessary.

It is like a house with two rooms. One is his room; you walk in, smell his clothes, and weep aloud. The other is the kitchen, where the children need to eat and the bills need to be paid. Today you laughed a little in the kitchen, and tomorrow you walk back into that room. There is nothing wrong with walking back and forth, and no one has set a rule for how long you should stay.

Most people slowly find a way to live with the loss, while some remain stuck for a long time. Psychiatry calls this prolonged grief disorder; it was added to the DSM-5-TR in 2022, and a 2017 meta-analysis estimated that about 10% of bereaved adults experience it, with a higher rate when the death was unnatural. If daily functioning is still hard after a long time, this does not mean your faith is not enough. Please seek professional help; it can be treated.
Can near-death experiences count as evidence?

The AWARE study by Sam Parnia, a British and American researcher (2014), collected 2,060 cases of cardiac arrest. Of the 140 survivors who completed interviews, 9% met the criteria for a near-death experience, 2% reported a clear memory of the resuscitation, and only 1 case could be partly verified. Among the 28 interviewees of AWARE-II (2023), no one recognized the visual images placed in the experiment, and 1 person passed the sound test. The authors suggest that some form of consciousness may continue during cardiac arrest. This is a phenomenon worth studying, but it does not prove a world after death.

Christians must be even more careful. The best-selling book The Boy Who Came Back from Heaven was pulled by the publisher Tyndale in January 2015, because the person at its center publicly said that he had not died and had not gone to heaven, and that he had been lying. The Christian hope is built on the historical witness to Jesus’ resurrection, not on near-death stories.
Bringing death back among the living

Cicely Saunders, the pioneer of the modern hospice movement, was a Christian and founded St Christopher’s Hospice in London in 1967. She proposed “total pain”: suffering has physical, emotional, social and spiritual dimensions. She had meant to run a church institution, but it was opened to people of every faith and of none. The surgeon Atul Gawande (Being Mortal, 2014) argues that medicine should not only ask how to prolong life, but also what matters to the patient. A 2010 randomized trial of 151 lung cancer patients showed that those who received palliative care early had a better quality of life and less aggressive end-of-life treatment, with median survival of 11.6 months versus 8.9 months. This is a single study and not personal medical advice.
Death is the topic most often turned into stories, so we must be all the more careful to separate the facts.
Becker died of cancer on March 6, 1974, and The Denial of Death (1973) won the Pulitzer Prize two months after his death.
Kübler-Ross’s five stages came from her work with terminally ill patients; researchers argue that they are not suitable for prescribing how the bereaved should grieve.

Becker’s thought gave rise to terror management theory, but one representative experimental effect of that theory failed to replicate in Many Labs 4 in 2022 (17 labs, about 1,550 people). That people fear death is easy to observe; the mechanism is not settled.
Some survivors of cardiac arrest report a clear experience. These are real reports, but the current AWARE studies have not experimentally verified that “consciousness leaves the body.”

Death is an enemy, Christ has overcome it, and those who believe in Him will rise. This is the core declaration of the Christian faith, based on the witness to Jesus’ resurrection (see the Jesus Hall), and not a medical conclusion.
The viewpoint conversation room
What happens after we die? Below, each view is set out in its strongest form. The differences between them are real and should not be blurred together.

items.h: Consciousness ends with the brain, and there is no afterlife. Epicurus held that since we will not feel anything, there is nothing to fear; many people live earnestly on this basis. The challenge: do the people we love and all justice finally come to nothing?

The Hindu and Buddhist traditions each hold that life and death follow one another, and that the goal of practice is liberation. They take the consequences of actions seriously. The difference from Christianity lies in whether a person lives only once, and in what salvation depends on.

Death is an enemy, not a friend; Jesus’ resurrection is the first fruit of the future resurrection of the body. Evangelicals mostly believe that believers who die are with the Lord and await the resurrection of the body; on the details of the state in between there are differing understandings, but the core is in Christ.

blocks.h: The Bible does not prettify death
Some say death is just part of life. The Bible’s name for it is not polite:
The last enemy that will be abolished is death.

So Christians may weep. Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb, and in Gethsemane, facing His own death, He said to His disciples, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death.” The Bible asks people not to grieve “like the rest, who have no hope.” It does not say not to grieve.

But we don’t want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.
He walked in Himself
God’s eternal power is shown here in an unexpected way: He did not remove death from heaven. He became flesh and blood, died, and broke it from the inside.

Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”
He asked Martha, and He asks everyone today. He puts the hope in Himself, in a person, and not in a system of explanation.
“Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
When sins are forgiven, death has its sting pulled out. It will still come, and it will still break hearts, but it no longer has the last word.
For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.

Find a photo of a family member or a friend who has died and look at it quietly for one minute. Say to God one word of thanks or one thing you never got to say. If the person is still living, find a way to say it in person today.

Meditate: if I had only one year left, what would I stop and what would I start? Which part of death do I fear: the pain, unfinished business, leaving my family, or the unknown afterward? Tell the Lord concretely.

Prayer: Lord Jesus, who died and rose again, I admit that I am afraid, and that there are people I miss so much I cannot speak. Thank You for walking through death Yourself and coming back with the victory. Comfort those who are weeping, let us grieve without despair, and teach us to number our days and live today well. If someone tonight does not want to go on living, hold on to him, send someone to be with him, and let him speak up today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Shift your viewpoint: move from a temporary, earthly view to an eternal one, so that a phone call today or a single apology carries weight.
Relationships matter more than things: no one on his deathbed wants one more look at his bank book. While there is time, say the love out loud and untie the knots.
Selfless: there is no need to build immortality projects any more. Let Jesus receive all the glory, and whether my name will be remembered can be set down.

blocks.h: This week: do the thing most people keep putting off: have one “if the day comes” conversation with your family. What medical care do you want, who decides for you, and which hymn would you like at the farewell service? In Taiwan you can learn about advance decisions on medical care.
Pass it on: “If you could ask one question of someone who has come to the end of life, what would you ask?”
Quiz

quiz.q: From whose experience did Kübler-Ross’s five stages originally come, mainly?
o: A large experiment on the bereaved
Terminally ill patients
A questionnaire of university students
quiz.e: They were only later extended to the bereaved, and researchers have criticized using them to prescribe how to grieve.

quiz.q: About research on near-death experiences, which statement is the most accurate?
o: Science has proved that heaven exists
The survivors’ reports are all lies
There are real reports worth studying, but at present they are not enough to prove a world after death
quiz.e: The AWARE studies had very few verified cases; the ground of the Christian hope is Jesus’ resurrection.

quiz.q: How does 1 Thessalonians 4:13 view Christian grief?
o: Do not grieve like the rest, who have no hope
Christians should not grieve
Grief shows a lack of faith
quiz.e: The text does not forbid grief; it says this grief carries hope. Jesus Himself wept.

units.title: Loneliness: Made for Relationship
units.sub: You can be lonely too deep for words at a table full of relatives. This pain is telling you that you were made for relationship.

share.v: I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.

blocks.h: A 2025 report from the World Health Organization estimates that around the world 1 in 6 people is affected by loneliness, and that deaths associated with loneliness number more than 871,000 a year, about 100 every hour.

The Bible noticed this much earlier. In Genesis 1, again and again God looks at what He has made and calls it “good.” By chapter 2, the setting is perfect and sin has not yet entered, and yet God for the first time says: “not good.”
Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”
Lonely does not mean alone

The WHO definition is worth remembering: loneliness is the pain that comes from the gap between the relationships you want and the relationships you actually have, while social isolation is an objective lack of connections. So some people live alone and are at peace, and others are lonely beyond words in a marriage, in a church, or at a table full of relatives.

Loneliness is like thirst. Being thirsty does not mean you are defective; it is your body reminding you that it is time to drink water. Loneliness is a signal too, telling you: you are a person who needs relationships. It is hard to bear, but it is not your sin, and it does not prove that you have failed.
The body is keeping count too

A 2015 meta-analysis found that loneliness, social isolation and living alone were associated with about 26%, 29% and 32% higher likelihood of death respectively. Another analysis in 2023 pooled 90 cohort studies with about 2.2 million people and estimated about 32% for social isolation and about 14% for loneliness. The numbers run high and low, but the direction is consistent.

The 2023 advisory of the US Surgeon General used a comparison that spread widely: the effect of lacking social connection on the risk of early death can be as great as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. This is an analogy for the size of the risk, not a claim that the two work by the same mechanism.

Research has also found a heartbreaking cycle: lonely people become more alert to social threat and more likely to read other people’s silence as rejection, so they withdraw further and become lonelier still. A meta-analysis of intervention studies found that the overall effect is small, but methods that address such thoughts work better than simply adding opportunities for social contact. So “get out more” is often not enough; sometimes someone needs to help you reinterpret, and where necessary professional help is needed too.

Why do the numbers differ so much from place to place? Because the questions are asked differently. The US Surgeon General’s report says about half of adults have “experienced” loneliness; a 2022 BMJ review of data from 113 countries put the share of European adults at a “problematic level” at roughly 5% to 7% (5.3% for young people, 6.9% for the middle-aged), and low-income countries had no nationally representative adult data. When you read a headline about a “loneliness epidemic,” first ask: how was it measured?
Let us separate what is certain, what is under discussion, and what is inference.
Loneliness and social isolation are associated with a higher risk of death. This appears repeatedly in a number of large meta-analyses.

The WHO estimates that about one in six people worldwide is affected by loneliness, and that about 871,000 deaths a year are associated with loneliness. These are figures extrapolated from existing data, and the completeness of the data varies from place to place.

Addressing negative interpretations of social situations is currently one of the more effective ways of reducing loneliness; but the overall effect is on the small side, and research here is still accumulating.
The direction of causation has not been fully sorted out. People cannot be randomly assigned to isolation, so most studies are observational; poor health can also make people lonelier.

People’s longing for relationship fits very well with the belief that “God Himself is a fellowship of love and made human beings in His own image.” This is a theological inference; science has not proved it and cannot.
The viewpoint conversation room
Why do people get lonely? These views are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

items.h: Human beings could survive only through a safe and reliable group, so loneliness, like hunger, is a signal that urges a person back to the group. This explanation does not need to mention God, and a good deal of research supports it.
Human beings were made in the image of the triune God, and so they long to be known and loved. The pain of loneliness points to the purpose for which people were made.
Many Christian scholars hold that God can shape the human body and emotions through natural processes. An explanation of the mechanism and an explanation of the purpose answer different questions.

blocks.h: He lived in love before creation

If God were alone in eternity, then “love” would have to wait until there was a world to have an object. What the Christian faith says is that the one true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, has loved one another from eternity. Jesus’ prayer before His arrest reveals this secret.
Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world.

God did not make people because He was lonely; He is full of love, and so He invites people in. Your loneliness is not a design flaw. The empty place in the human heart that needs others was left there at creation.
He entered the deepest abandonment
On the cross, the disciples had scattered, the crowd was mocking, and Jesus cried out loudly the words of Psalm 22.
At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” which is, being interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

So you do not have to explain to Jesus what it means that no one understands. He bore our sins and walked through that darkness, and then rose from the dead, and so He can say this to everyone who trusts in Him:
For he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”

Exactly what this “forsaken” means is understood by theologians at greater and lesser depth: most evangelical theologians hold that Jesus truly bore the judgment and separation that come from sin, while also reminding us that the essence of the Trinity was not thereby divided. This is a mystery, and there is no need to hurry to exhaust it.
Single people are not half persons

The immediate context of Genesis 2:18 is marriage, but it does not say that single people are incomplete. Jesus never married, and Paul had no spouse during his ministry, and both lived fully. Marriage is not the cure for loneliness, as many married people can testify. God’s answer is wider than marriage: He places people into a family.
Looking around at those who sat around him, he said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother.”

Open the contacts on your phone and scroll slowly through. Which name makes your heart tighten? Whom have you not been in touch with for a long time? Notice also one time of day: when are you most lonely in a day? Tell Jesus that time directly.
Meditate: what is my loneliness calling out for? Have I locked myself in tighter than others have shut me out, for fear of being rejected?

Prayer: Lord Jesus, You were abandoned by everyone, and You understand me. I hand You the loneliness I cannot put into words. Thank You for promising never to leave me. Give me courage to open up to others, and open my eyes to see the people around me who are just as lonely. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The 235 relationships: spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, spiritual comrades. You do not need all three at once; first pray and ask God to give you one companion.
Relationships matter more than things: take a little of your phone-scrolling time for one real phone call. A “like” is not the same as being present.
Humility overcomes pride: “I’m doing fine” is sometimes a wall. Saying “I need you” is the beginning of taking the wall down.

blocks.h: If you are really struggling: if loneliness is so heavy that you feel you cannot go on, or if the low mood has lasted for several weeks, please tell someone you trust today and seek help from a doctor or counselor. In Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925 or Lifeline 1995; elsewhere there are local resources too. Asking for help is not weakness, and it does not mean your faith is lacking.

This week: invite one person to a meal or make a 20-minute phone call, preferably to someone you think may be lonely too (an older person living alone, a single parent, a new friend). No need for big ideas. Just ask, “How have you been lately?” and then listen.
Pass it on: “Have you ever felt very lonely even though you were surrounded by people? Why do you think people need so much to be understood?”
Quiz

quiz.q: How does the World Health Organization describe “loneliness”?
o: The pain from the gap between the relationships you want and the relationships you actually have
Living alone
Having fewer than five friends
quiz.e: Loneliness is a subjective gap; social isolation is the objective lack of connections.

quiz.q: About research on loneliness and risk of death, which statement is the most accurate?
o: It has been proved that loneliness always kills
Studies show that loneliness is associated with risk of death, and the direction of cause is still not fully sorted out
Loneliness has nothing to do with health
quiz.e: Meta-analyses repeatedly find an association, but most of the studies are observational.

quiz.q: In Mark 3:34-35 in this unit, whom does Jesus call His brothers, sisters and mother?
o: Only blood relatives
Only married disciples
Whoever does the will of God
quiz.e: God places people into a family, and the single and the married both have a share.

units.title: Shame and Sin
units.sub: Guilt says, “I did something wrong.” Shame says, “I am wrong.” The gospel answers these two sentences differently.

share.v: There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus

blocks.h: The first new garment in human history was a garment to cover shame, and the first game of hide-and-seek was played with God.

After human beings sinned, the Bible records their first reaction without any mention of repentance or argument. It records only two actions: cover up, and hide. Thousands of years later, when you and I fail an exam, go through a divorce, lose a job, or are talked about behind our backs, our hands are still doing the same two things.
Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
“I did something wrong” and “I am wrong”

In a 2007 review article, the psychologist June Tangney and colleagues set out the distinction now widely accepted, which can be traced back to Helen Block Lewis in 1971: shame is a negative evaluation of the whole self, and guilt is a negative evaluation of a specific behavior. Shame usually hurts more, because the one being judged is “me.”

The two also lead to different behavior. Overall, research shows that guilt more often leads to admitting wrong, apologizing and making amends; people prone to shame more often want to deny, hide or flee, and more often show anger, blaming others, depression and low self-esteem.

Guilt is like a warning light on a car: something is wrong here, so take it to be fixed. Shame is like someone walking up and saying to you, “This car was always scrap metal.” The first makes you look for a repair shop, while the second makes you want to hide the car in the garage and never drive it out again.

The social work scholar Brené Brown studies shame through interviews and describes it as an intense pain, the belief that one is flawed and therefore unworthy of love and belonging. Among her “shame resilience” elements is reaching out to others and telling the story. The subjects of her 2006 study were women, and her starting point was not faith, but this observation is well worth the church’s hearing.
Do the Chinese have only “face,” and only the West a conscience?

The saying “the East is a shame culture and the West is a guilt culture” has spread widely, and it comes from the anthropologist Ruth Benedict’s The Chrysanthemum and the Sword (1946). The book came out of her analysis for the US Office of War Information during World War II; she could not do fieldwork in Japan at that time and relied mainly on documents, films and interviews.

Later criticism has been abundant. C. Douglas Lummis argued that she portrayed Japan as a classless, unchanging society; Millie Creighton in 1990 reviewed the forty-year-long discussion. Putting a single label on a whole civilization is no longer a safe thing to say today.

The Chinese language itself is a counterexample. In 2004 O. A. Bedford, working with Taiwanese respondents, analyzed 4 Chinese terms for shame (diūliǎn 丟臉 “losing face,” cánkuì 慚愧 “feeling ashamed,” xiūkuì 羞愧 “ashamed,” xiūchǐ 羞恥 “shame”) and 3 terms for guilt (nèijiù 內疚 “inner guilt,” zuì’è gǎn 罪惡感 “a sense of guilt,” fànzuì gǎn 犯罪感 “a sense of having offended”). The Chinese not only have the sting of conscience; they distinguish its kinds very finely.
The Chinese word for “sin” has a translation problem

Many friends, on hearing “you are a sinner,” react first with: “But I haven’t broken the law.” The Chinese word for sin, zui (罪), easily calls to mind courts and prisons. The sin the Bible speaks of is broader and closer to relationship: leaving God, not letting God be God, putting oneself at the center. A law-abiding good person can also live a whole life that has no need of God.
In which language should the gospel be told?

items.h: The scholar Jackson Wu argues in Saving God’s Face that in presenting salvation to Chinese people we should give weight to the language of honor and shame: the heart of sin is shaming God, and Christ’s redemption restores God’s honor and also gives believers a new identity.

Traditional evangelical teaching stresses law, guilt and justification: people have violated God’s justice, and Christ was punished in their place. This path is also deeply rooted in Romans, and it has brought many Chinese people to faith. The reviewer G. Wright Doyle criticizes Wu for underestimating the weight of law in the Bible and in Chinese history.

Many pastors hold that the Bible uses many pictures at once, including the courtroom, the family, the temple, and honor and shame, and that we need not choose only one. The gospel both forgives guilt and removes shame.

blocks.h: All of these views acknowledge the cross of Christ as the only foundation of salvation. The difference lies in how it is expressed and emphasized. Here they are set side by side without a verdict.
Layering the statements keeps research, interpretation and faith from being mixed together.
Psychological research generally distinguishes shame (directed at the whole self) from guilt (directed at a specific behavior). This is currently the most dominant way of defining them.

Proneness to shame is associated with depression, anger and withdrawal; guilt more often leads to making amends. These are mainly correlational studies and cannot be stated directly as causes; and if guilt and shame are mixed together, guilt can also hurt.

The dichotomy that treats East Asia as a “shame culture” and the West as a “guilt culture” has been influential but has drawn a great deal of criticism from scholars. The Chinese vocabulary of both shame and guilt is quite rich.
Crucifixion in the Roman world was not only cruel but was regarded as extremely shameful. This is the mainstream view in studies of the New Testament background.

In the parable of the prodigal son, the father running was an undignified act in traditional Middle Eastern society. This is an interpretation proposed by Kenneth Bailey on the basis of Middle Eastern culture and adopted by many expositors; the text does not say it explicitly.

The deepest root of shame is that human beings left their relationship with God, and Christ on the cross personally bore human disgrace. This is a theological judgment that psychology can neither prove nor refute.
He comes first to find the one who hid
The most moving thing in Genesis 3 is a question. After the human beings hid, God did not wait for them to come out by themselves.
Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
He of course knew where they were. This sentence is an open door. At the end of the story, the fig-leaf skirts that they made themselves are replaced: God Himself made clothes for them.
Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
Self-centered: the root beneath the leaves

The serpent’s line was “you will be like God.” The root of the fall was leaving the creature’s place and wanting to be God oneself. This is what we call being self-centered: centered on me, and then having to maintain an image of “I’m fine.” Pride and shame are really two sides of the same coin, both keeping their eyes fixed on the self.
Shame on the cross

Christ went in the opposite direction: being in the form of God, He “emptied himself.” On the cross He was reviled by the crowd, who wagged their heads and mocked. This was the most shameful road, and yet He went up with His eyes open.
looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
So the gospel has an answer for sin and an answer for shame. To guilt, He says: forgiven. To shame, He says: I come to stand with you, and I call you “children.”
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
If it was not your fault

There is a kind of shame that comes from what others have done to you: being assaulted, abused at home, bullied, abandoned. In the Bible, Tamar was raped by her half-brother, and she put ashes on her head and wept aloud, while her family told her to hold her peace. The Bible records this plainly, and it puts the word “folly” on the one who committed the deed.

Please hear this clearly: being a victim is not a sin, and it does not need repentance. That shame was laid on you by someone else’s evil, and you do not have to confess it as your own sin. God’s justice stands on the side of the victim.

Take out your phone, open your notes, and write down the one thing you least want anyone to know, or write just one word to stand for it. You do not need to show it to anyone. Then bring it before God.
Meditate: God asked in the garden, “Where are you?” If He asked you today, what would you be hiding behind? Busyness, achievements, a smile, or “I’m fine”?

Prayer: Heavenly Father, I often hide. For the things I have done wrong I come to confess, and I ask You to forgive, and to help me apologize and make amends. As for the hurt and disgrace that others laid on me, I will not carry it for them any more; please heal me Yourself. Thank You that Jesus despised the shame and went to the cross for me. Today I am willing to step out from behind the leaves. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Self-centered to selfless: shame and pride both keep your eyes fixed on yourself. Turn your gaze to Christ and you no longer need to manage an image.

Jesus is my example: He did not define Himself by others’ evaluations, and He did not shame those who failed. At home and in small groups, first put away the sentence “how could you be so disgraceful.”
Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the church must not govern people by shame. Confession is for healing, not for public execution.

blocks.h: If you have been hurt: if you are suffering domestic violence, sexual assault or any abuse, your safety comes first; this is not your fault, and you do not need to endure it. In Taiwan you can call the 113 Protection Hotline; elsewhere, please contact your local protection agency. If shame is so heavy that you feel you cannot go on living, please tell someone you trust today and seek professional help; in Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925 or Lifeline 1995.

This week: tell apart one thing that is hard for you: is it “I did something wrong” (go and confess, apologize, make amends), or “someone hurt me” (go and tell a trusted person or a professional)? Then say a small part of it to someone trustworthy.
Pass it on: “Have you noticed that what people fear most is often not doing wrong but being found out? How do you think a person can truly let go of that feeling of disgrace?”
Quiz

quiz.q: According to the mainstream psychological distinction, what is the biggest difference between shame and guilt?
o: Shame is felt only by Easterners and guilt only by Westerners
Shame is directed at the whole self and guilt at a specific behavior
Shame is milder and guilt is more serious
quiz.e: Shame says “I am wrong,” and guilt says “I did something wrong.” Both exist in every culture.

quiz.q: What does this unit say about the shame felt by those who were assaulted or abused by others?
o: Being a victim is not a sin and needs no repentance; first make sure of safety and seek help
They should confess it as sin and learn to endure
Do not mention it; it is best to keep quiet for the time being
quiz.e: That evil was laid on you by someone else. That Tamar was told to “hold her peace” is a tragedy the Bible records, not a teaching.

quiz.q: How does Hebrews 12:2 say Jesus faced the cross?
o: He could not feel the shame
He got through on the respect of the crowd
For the joy set before Him, He despised the shame
quiz.e: He did not avoid the shame; for the joy that was set before Him, He overcame it.

units.title: Are Money and Success Enough?
units.sub: Lottery winners really are more satisfied with life years later. So why did Jesus call the rich man a “fool”?

share.v: He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”

blocks.h: If you won the lottery next month, would you be happier than you are now ten or more years later? A few Swedish economists actually went and asked. They surveyed big-prize winners between 5 and 22 years after the win and compared them with a control group in similar circumstances.

The result may differ from what you heard in Sunday school: the winners’ satisfaction with life as a whole stayed higher, with no clear fading after more than a decade. But the gap in their happiness and mental health was much smaller. Money bought something, and there was something it did not buy.
He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he who loves abundance, with increase. This also is vanity.
First, an honest word: money helps

In 2010 the Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton analyzed more than 450,000 Gallup survey responses in the United States and reached a widely quoted result: people’s evaluation of their lives kept rising with income, while their day-to-day mood stopped improving at an annual income of about US$75,000.

In 2021 Matthew Killingsworth collected more than a million real-time reports through a phone app and found that mood kept rising with income. The two sides did not trade blows. They sat down and reanalyzed the data together. Their 2023 conclusion: only the least happy group levels off after a certain income, while everyone else’s happiness keeps rising roughly with the logarithm of income.

Think of “logarithm” as your phone’s battery. Charge it from 1% to 20% and you come back to life: calls go through and the map works. Charge it from 80% to 100% and you simply feel a little more secure. That is what logarithmic means: to feel one more notch of the same happiness, your income has to double again. So for someone still at 1%, money is a lifeline, and nobody should lecture that person about being above it all.

The Lausanne Movement’s Theology Working Group says the same in its statement from Akropong, Africa: the Bible includes material well-being within God’s blessing, and God takes no pleasure in people living in poverty. Poverty is neither a virtue nor a curse.
Why is it still not enough?

When a phone’s navigation reaches the destination, it just says, “You have arrived.” And then? The navigation of life jumps to the next stop by itself. You passed the entrance exam, so the next stop is a good job. You became a manager, so the next stop is director. You bought a house, so the next stop is a bigger one. Every stretch of the road is taken seriously, yet the engine never gets switched off.

Psychologists call this adaptation. In 1978 Philip Brickman and colleagues interviewed lottery winners and people who had suffered serious accidents, and found that the winners were not as happy as one might imagine and took less pleasure in everyday things. That study’s sample was small, and the large Swedish study mentioned above corrected it: adaptation is not complete, and the benefits of money can last. A fairer way to put it is that people gradually get used to what they have, and financial satisfaction and inner joy are two different lines.
Staking your life on money is not the same as having money

A 2014 meta-analysis found that the more people value wealth and possessions, the lower their subjective well-being tends to be. This is a correlation and the direction may run both ways: anxious people may also grip their possessions harder. Research also links spending money on others with well-being, a pattern seen in rich and poor countries alike.
The Chinese version: success for whom?

The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiaojing) says in its opening chapter: “To establish oneself and walk in the Way, to make one’s name known to later generations and so bring honor to one’s parents: this is the final stage of filial piety.” It is a beautiful expression of gratitude, and it can also become a very heavy load. The Taiwanese psychologist Kuang-Hui Yeh and his colleague Olwen Bedford distinguish two kinds of filial piety: reciprocal filial piety, which grows out of affection and repays love, and authoritarian filial piety, which grows out of role and authority. Many children choose their exam track, their study abroad, their major and their spouse as if repaying a debt on behalf of the whole family. Being grateful to our parents is a blessing. Letting a report card decide whether a person is worthy of love is not what filial piety was meant to be.

items.h: At its strongest, it points out that God really does delight to bless and that the Bible contains material promises.
